title: KCD-CAM: A K-Nearest-Neighbor Accelerator Based on Charge-Domain Content-Addressable-Memory for Point Cloud Processing
evidence_span: KCD-CAM uses a 4T2R ReRAM charge-domain CAM for in-situ range search, corner-clipped iterative top-k search, and dual-granularity voxel hashing; real-world point-cloud benchmarks report 279.79x speed and 3282x energy-efficiency gains over GPU implementations, plus 8.51x speed and 4.76x energy-efficiency gains over state-of-the-art KNN accelerators.
problem: Euclidean-distance top-k KNN search dominates point-cloud processing cost and prevents real-time efficient edge execution.
method_or_artifact: ReRAM charge-domain CAM KNN accelerator with in-situ range search, iterative top-k selection, and dual-granularity voxel hashing.
workload_or_benchmark: Real-world 3D point-cloud datasets and KNN processing; dataset names, point counts, accuracy criteria, device parameters, and GPU baselines are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: 4T2R ReRAM CAM with charge-domain computation and edge point-cloud processing; array size, ADC/sensing, process, voltage, and data-movement boundaries are unspecified.
metrics: 3282x greater energy efficiency than GPU implementations
8.51x speed improvement over state-of-the-art KNN accelerators
4.76x energy-efficiency improvement over state-of-the-art KNN accelerators
limits: The description omits accuracy/recall tradeoffs, end-to-end preprocessing, ADC/peripheral costs, technology details, and measurement boundaries.
Large relative gains may depend on GPU and accelerator baseline configurations and whether data movement is included.
Official description only; performance and energy claims require paper-level hardware verification.

title: DFA-DRIVE: A Cross-Layer Delay Fault Analysis and Optimization Framework for Robust Multi-Task Driving Perception
evidence_span: DFA-DRIVE propagates temperature-induced timing failures from circuit analysis through object detection, drivable-area segmentation, and lane-line segmentation, then DFA-OPT remaps DNN layers across systolic-array resources; under AEC-Q100 Grade 0/1 envelopes, small arrays retain near-baseline accuracy when 256x256 arrays lose up to 4% at 150C, with comparable accuracy using up to 92% fewer cycles.
problem: Temperature, voltage droop, and aging induce delay faults in automotive DNN accelerators, creating task-level perception degradation in safety-critical driving systems.
method_or_artifact: Cross-layer delay-fault propagation analysis and adaptive thermal-sensitivity-aware DNN hardware mapping.
workload_or_benchmark: Multi-task driving perception covering detection, drivable-area segmentation, and lane-line segmentation across AEC-Q100 Grade 0 and Grade 1 temperature envelopes; model, fault injection, and baseline mapping details are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: DNN systolic arrays ranging from 4x4 to 256x256 under automotive temperatures of -40C to 150C or 125C; process, thermal model, voltage, frequency, and sensor pipeline are unspecified.
metrics: Up to 4% accuracy drop for 256x256 arrays at 150C
Comparable accuracy with up to 92% fewer computation cycles using adaptive mapping
limits: The description omits task-specific accuracy, timing-fault distributions, thermal transients, power/area cost, and comparison mapping details.
Near-baseline accuracy under selected conditions does not establish safety certification or robustness across vehicles and workloads.
Official description only; automotive reliability claims require paper-level fault and thermal validation.

title: Graph-Based Attack-Chain Traceback Across Multiple In-Vehicle Network Domains
evidence_span: The gateway-resident system reconstructs multi-stage vehicle attack chains from IDS alerts across host, Ethernet, and CAN domains using temporal graphs constrained by topological, temporal, semantic, and kinematic plausibility; on a production Leapmotor C10 it reports 0.90 edge F1, 0.086 false-discovery rate, 1.2% CPU, and 26 MB memory, and releases a traceback dataset.
problem: Connected vehicles require multi-stage attack traceback, but packet marking can violate UN R155 and ISO/SAE 21434 certification boundaries and production resources are constrained.
method_or_artifact: Certification-compatible gateway traceback using temporal graphs over existing cross-domain IDS alerts and four plausibility checks.
workload_or_benchmark: Multi-domain in-vehicle attack traceback evaluated on a production Leapmotor C10; attack scenarios, alert corpus, baseline methods, and dataset split are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Production vehicle gateway spanning host, Ethernet, and CAN domains with limited CPU/memory; vehicle software, IDS configuration, and certification process are unspecified.
metrics: 1.2% CPU and 26 MB memory on production vehicle
limits: The description omits recall breakdown, attack coverage, alert quality, latency, vehicle generality, and certification evidence.
Performance on one vehicle and released dataset does not establish robustness across OEM architectures or IDS deployments.
Official description only; security and compliance claims require paper-level and independent dataset verification.

title: Enabling Robust On-Device Personalization via Pulse-Based Mapping and Noise Suppression for Non-Ideal CIM Architecture
evidence_span: CIM-MP co-optimizes hardware and software for in-situ personalization under noisy CIM updates using pulse-based weight mapping, Feature Variation Elimination during forward propagation, and Gradient Adaptive Purification during backpropagation; experiments report up to 35.1% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art approaches.
problem: Analog CIM weights are expensive to read and transfer for external fine-tuning, while non-ideal device noise makes direct on-device personalization unstable.
method_or_artifact: Pulse-based in-memory update mapping with feature-noise suppression and gradient purification for robust CIM fine-tuning.
workload_or_benchmark: On-device deep-model personalization under non-ideal CIM conditions; model/task suite, device noise model, training budget, and state-of-the-art baselines are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Analog CIM arrays supporting in-situ weight updates and noisy forward/backward computation; device technology, ADC/DAC, pulse programming, endurance, and peripheral overhead are unspecified.
metrics: Up to 35.1% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art approaches
limits: The description omits absolute accuracy, task/model, convergence cost, energy, update endurance, and noise distributions.
Accuracy improvement may depend on the selected baseline and simulated rather than measured device behavior.
Official description only; learning and hardware claims require paper-level device-aware verification.

title: ATLAS: AI-Assisted Threat-to-Assertion Learning for System-on-Chip Security Verification
evidence_span: ATLAS maps CWE knowledge to SoC assets, weaknesses, assertion-based security properties, and JasperGold scripts; on three HACK@DAC benchmarks it detects 39 of 48 CWEs and generates correct properties for 33 of those 39 bugs.
problem: Translating standardized threat reasoning into SoC-specific formal security properties is labor-intensive and blocks secure-by-design verification.
method_or_artifact: LLM-driven asset-centric threat mapping and automatic generation of assertion properties and JasperGold verification scripts.
workload_or_benchmark: Three HACK@DAC security-verification benchmarks containing 48 CWE instances; benchmark composition, property correctness rubric, proof status, and comparison tools are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: System-on-Chip designs evaluated with formal property verification and JasperGold; RTL scale, threat model, solver settings, and human review process are unspecified.
metrics: 33/39 detected bugs receive correct generated properties
limits: The description omits false negatives by CWE, proof completion, assertion soundness, generated-script failures, and human adjudication effort.
Benchmark results may not generalize to unseen SoC architectures, CWE variants, or proprietary threat models.
Official description only; LLM-generated verification claims require artifact and formal-proof inspection.
